title: Knowing God from Creation
lead: Can people know something of God from the world he made and from their own conscience, without the Bible? Psalm 19 and Romans 1–2 say yes; the churches disagree about how much this knowledge can do. Catholic teaching holds that God can be known with certainty from creation; Reformed and Lutheran teaching holds that it leaves people without excuse but cannot save; Karl Barth rejected natural theology altogether.

sections.b: Psalm 19 says the heavens recount God's glory. Paul tells the people of Lystra and Athens that God has not left himself without witness and that people are meant to seek him (Acts 14:15–17; 17:22–31). In Romans 1:19–20 God's invisible qualities are seen in what he made, and in 2:14–15 Gentiles show the work of the law written on their hearts. The Wisdom of Solomon makes the same argument at length.
sections.refs: Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:15–17; Acts 17:22–31; Romans 1:19–20; Romans 2:14–15; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1–9

sections.b: The Greek fathers took over the Stoic idea of a natural law; Augustine used it against Pelagius and for it; Aquinas built on it; Calvin spoke of a sense of divinity in every person, darkened by sin; Vatican I defined that God can be known from creation by natural reason; Barth's "No!" to Brunner (1934) denied that there is a point of contact in human nature for the gospel.
